{{Short description|American theoretical physicist}}
[[File:Gregory Moore 2012.jpg|thumb|250px|Gregory Moore, 2012]]
'''Gregory W. Moore''' is an American [[theoretical physicist]] who specializes in [[mathematical physics]] and [[string theory]]. Moore is a professor in the Physics and Astronomy Department of [[Rutgers University]] and a member of the university's High Energy Theory group.<ref>[http://www.physics.rutgers.edu/~gmoore/ Gregory W. Moore homepage], Physics and Astronomy Department, Rutgers University</ref>

==Education==
Moore received an AB in physics from [[Princeton University]] in 1982 and a PhD in the same subject from [[Harvard University]] in 1985.<ref>{{cite web|title=2014 Dannie Heineman Prize for Mathematical Physics Recipient|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Moore&first_nm=Gregory&year=2014|access-date=25 January 2018}}</ref>

==Career==
Moore's research has focused on: [[D-branes]] on [[Calabi–Yau manifold]]s and BPS state counting; relations to [[Borcherds products]], [[automorphic forms]], black-hole entropy, and [[wall-crossing]]; applications of the theory of automorphic forms to [[conformal field theory]], string compactification, black hole entropy counting, and the [[AdS/CFT correspondence]]; potential relation between string theory and [[number theory]]; effective low energy [[supergravity]] theories in string compactification and the computation of nonperturbative stringy effects in effective supergravities; topological field theories, and applications to invariants of manifolds; [[string cosmology]] and [[string field theory]].

Moore was a member of the advisory board for [[Springer-Verlag|Springer's]]  ''Encyclopedia of Mathematical Physics''.<ref>[https://www.springer.com/physics/book/978-1-4020-5050-3?detailsPage=contentItemPage&CIPageCounter=543309 Editorial Board & Advisory Board]{{dead link|date=March 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}, ''Encyclopedia of Mathematical Physics'', [[Springer-Verlag]]. Accessed January 28, 2010</ref>

In 2008, he as well as [[Davide Gaiotto]] and [[Andrew Neitzke]] gave an alternative construction of the [[Ooguri–Vafa metric]], which was first constructed with the [[Gibbons–Hawking ansatz]].

==Awards==
Moore won a 2007 Essays on Gravitation Award from the Gravity Research Foundation for his essay, joint with [[Frederik Denef]], ''How Many Black Holes Fit on the Head of a Pin?'' <ref>[http://news.rutgers.edu/focus/issue.2007-09-26.1066478179/article.2007-09-26.5912297852?print Awards and recognition] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110720112915/http://news.rutgers.edu/focus/issue.2007-09-26.1066478179/article.2007-09-26.5912297852?print |date=2011-07-20 }}, Rutgers Focus, September 26, 2007. Accessed January 28, 2010</ref><ref>[http://www.gravityresearchfoundation.org/winners_year.html#07 Awards by Year.] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070929022056/http://www.gravityresearchfoundation.org/winners_year.html |date=2007-09-29 }} Gravity Research Foundation. Accessed January 28, 2010</ref> In 2012 he became a fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>[https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society], retrieved 2013-02-10.</ref>

Moore won the 2014 Dannie Heineman Prize for Mathematical Physics "For eminent contributions to mathematical physics with a wide influence in many fields, ranging from string theory to supersymmetric gauge theory, conformal field theory, condensed matter physics and four-manifold theory."<ref>{{cite web|title=2014 Dannie Heineman Prize for Mathematical Physics|url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Moore&first_nm=Gregory&year=2014}}</ref> In 2015, he was jointly awarded the 2015 [[Dirac Medal (ICTP)|Dirac Medal]] by [[ICTP]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://gonitsora.com/2015-dirac-medallists-announced/|title=2015 Dirac Medallists Announced|first=Manjil|last=Saikia|publisher=Gonitsora|date=2015-08-10|access-date=2016-03-27}}</ref>

Moore was elected as a member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 2011 and a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 2020.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Gregory Winthrop Moore|url=https://www.amacad.org/person/gregory-winthrop-moore|website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences|language=en|access-date=2020-05-10}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=2020 NAS Election|url=http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2020-nas-election.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200428010617/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2020-nas-election.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 28, 2020|website=www.nasonline.org|access-date=2020-05-10}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Moore is married to [[Karin M. Rabe]], and son of [[Arthur Cotton Moore]].{{citation needed|date=January 2021}}
